name: Australia
sources: GDP $311bn: World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series AUS, 1990 - the print is $311,840,666,465, on the same series as the rest of the roster. Cross-check: Australian nominal GDP was near A$395bn in 1990 and the year's average rate about US$0.78 to the Australian dollar, which gives roughly $308bn. The two agree within 1%, which is a better result than Spain's or Canada's and is worth stating because it is the case where the convention costs nothing.
Population 17.1m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series AUS, 1990 = 17,065,128. The census of 6 August 1991 counted 16,850,540 on a night-of basis.

Inflation 7.3%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, series AUS, 1990 = 7.33%. This is the highest inflation of any of the four Anglosphere democracies in the roster and the reason the interest rate below is what it is.

Interest rate 17.0%: the Reserve Bank cash rate as it stood in January 1990, which is the month the game starts. This is a start-of-game figure and deliberately not an annual average: the cash rate had peaked near 18% in 1989, stood about 17-17.5% in January 1990, and was cut through the year to roughly 12% by December as the recession Keating later called the one Australia had to have took hold. Entering the average would have understated the monetary stance the player inherits on turn one by five points. The coupled constraint: 0.025 - (0.170 - 0.073) = -0.072, inside the band and wider than Canada's, which is the right ordering - Australia was running the tightest money in the developed world at the start of 1990.

TFP trend 0.011: the highest of the three, and the reason is the reform programme that had been running since the dollar was floated in December 1983 - tariff cuts announced in 1988 and again in 1991, financial deregulation, the Accord holding real wages while it happened. Australian multifactor productivity growth did in fact accelerate through the 1990s to roughly 1.5% a year, which is the strongest productivity record in the Anglosphere in this period. Entered above Spain's 0.009 and Canada's 0.008. Same caveat as the other two files: tech/mod.rs rewrites this field every tick, so it seeds the technology state and is not the growth-calibration dial.

Revenue 35% of GDP: total general-government revenue, Commonwealth plus states plus local, on the OECD basis. Australia is a federation and the Commonwealth share alone is near 24%; the general-government figure is entered for the same reason as Canada's.

Gross public debt 22% of GDP: general government, 1990. This is the lowest debt ratio in the roster after Kuwait's and it is not an error - the Hawke government ran four consecutive Commonwealth budget surpluses from 1987-88 to 1990-91 and was retiring debt outright. It is the single figure that most distinguishes Australia from Canada and New Zealand, whose adjustments of the same decade were financed rather than paid for.

Military 2.1% of GDP: World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS, series AUS, 1990 = 2.08%. Strength 14 is an index: about 70,000 permanent ADF personnel, built under the 1987 Defence of Australia white paper for exactly one job - denying the sea-air gap to Australia's north. Six Oberon submarines, four guided-missile frigates, 75 F/A-18s and 22 F-111Cs with genuine regional reach, and no capacity to sustain a land force anywhere. Indexed slightly above Canada's 12 for the strike and maritime patrol capability and below Spain's 16, which had four times the personnel.

Investment 27.6% of GDP: World Bank NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS, series AUS, 1990 = 27.62%, the highest ratio of any nation in this roster outside East Asia and a genuine feature of the late-1980s Australian boom rather than an artefact. The split entered here, 5.0 public and 22.6 private, is an apportionment and not a transcription: the series does not decompose by sector. Public gross fixed capital formation ran near 5% of GDP because government business enterprises - Telecom, the state electricity commissions, the railways - were still on the public balance sheet in 1990 and had not yet been corporatised or sold. The total is sourced; the split is reasoned.

Oil 0.6 mbd: crude oil and condensate production, chiefly the Gippsland Basin in Bass Strait and the North West Shelf, which came on stream through the late 1980s. FLAGGED AS THE WEAKEST NUMBER IN THIS FILE: I could not retrieve the 1990 print itself. What anchors it is that Australian production peaked at 802,000 barrels a day in 2000 and that Bass Strait alone averaged 450,000 barrels a day at its own 1985 peak, so a 1990 figure somewhat above that and well below the 2000 peak is the shape of the series. Entered at 0.6 as a stated estimate, not as a transcription, and it should be replaced the moment somebody has the Statistical Review page open.

Stability 76: the highest in the roster after the states with no opposition to be unstable against, and Australia earns it. Hawke won a fourth term on 24 March 1990 - eleven weeks after the game starts - with the Accord holding wages down by agreement with the unions rather than by law, a settled federation, and compulsory voting producing turnout above 94%. Marked below a hypothetical ceiling because Keating's leadership challenge was already being organised and would come in June 1991.

Separatism 0.04: below Italy's 0.05 and far below Canada's 0.38. What exists is real but small - Western Australian secessionism, which actually won a referendum 68-32 in 1933 and has never entirely gone away, and unresolved Aboriginal land rights, which in 1990 had produced the Barunga Statement of 1988 and Hawke's undelivered promise of a treaty. Mabo was two years away and Native Title four; neither is a secession movement, and neither is scheduled here.

Authoritarianism 0.06: the lowest in the roster. A written constitution amendable only by national referendum, High Court judicial review, a federation of six states, and an elected Senate under proportional representation that in living memory had blocked supply and brought a government down. Australia has more veto points than any other democracy on this board, which is what this number measures.

pop_growth_1990 = 1.5375%/yr. Compound annual growth of World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series AUS (Australia): 15,579,391 in 1984 to 16,814,416 in 1989 — the five years ending on the eve of the 1 January 1990 start date. See EconomyRecord::pop_growth_1990 in spheres-sim/src/data/mod.rs for why the window ends in 1989 and not with the single-year 1990 rate.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

ALL 48 OF THE 1990-ELIGIBLE TECHNOLOGIES WERE RULED FOR THIS NATION, one at a time, against a standard published per technology rather than per country. 13 were held and are listed below with their citations; 35 were refused. The refused ids are named at the end of this note so that a reader can tell a cell that was examined and refused from a cell nobody looked at - those are different claims and the schema would otherwise flatten them into the same silence.

RULED AND REFUSED, ids only (the reasoning for each refusal is held with the board that wrote it, one standard per technology): core_packet_internetworking, core_single_mode_fiber, core_carbon_composites, core_combined_cycle_turbine, comp_risc_superscalar, comm_fibre_optic_backbone, comm_geostationary_comsat, ener_seismic_3d_imaging, ener_horizontal_drilling, ener_gas_turbine_combined_cycle, matl_semiconductor_lithography, matl_composite_structures, matl_industrial_robotics, matl_lean_production, matl_single_crystal_superalloy, matl_rare_earth_magnet, matl_stereolithography, aero_precision_munitions, aero_pulse_doppler_radar, aero_stealth_shaping, aero_quiet_submarine, aero_recon_satellite, bio_oral_rehydration, bio_conjugate_vaccine, bio_automated_sequencing, tran_container_intermodal, tran_post_panamax_ship, tran_high_speed_rail, agri_drip_irrigation, agri_composite_membrane, agri_conservation_tillage, agri_integrated_pest_management, agri_protected_cultivation, agri_tissue_culture_propagation, agri_flue_gas_desulphurisation.

COLLISION RESOLVED. Two authoring boards ruled the same cell for this nation and disagreed. The tie-break is uniform across the whole roster and is not a preference between authors: the cell belongs to the board that owns the technology's domain in the registry, which for every non-core id is also its id prefix, and which both cross-domain authors published as their own deferral. core_packet_internetworking -> NOT HELD (semiconductors-computing said held, telecom-space said not held; resolved to the board that owns the Communications domain, telecom-space).

SECOND AUTHORING PASS, 2026-08-31, USE-SIDE ONLY. The first pass was correctly instructed to rule NOT HELD when unsure, and produced a defensible but ragged board: the convergence channel was reading that transcription's INCOMPLETENESS as this nation's IGNORANCE, and paying it to catch up to things it already had. A second pass therefore re-ruled the 31 USE-SIDE nodes against an explicit standard published before any nation was looked at, each limb written separately into every source string. LIMB A: a citable fact putting the technology in general commercial or public service across the OECD on or before 31 December 1989, asserted once per technology and identical for every nation. LIMB B: the nation is in the Advanced Set - 1990 OECD member AND World Bank high-income in the 1990 groupings AND one of the 29 authored majors: australia canada france germany italy japan netherlands spain sweden switzerland uk usa. LIMB C: a performed and RECORDED search for a named fact placing the nation outside that deployment; a silent limb C is a failed limb C. Where limb A failed for a technology the board said so and fell back to the first pass's named-artefact bar rather than granting on the class claim - which is why several second-pass refusals contradict the brief's own opening cut. THE SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE BAR IS UNCHANGED: producing a jet engine is still producing a jet engine, and not one of the 17 sovereignty-side ids was added, removed or re-reasoned by this pass. THE PASS IS ADDITIONS-ONLY - no first-pass grant was removed or weakened - and it was authored blind of model output, with the simulation never run and no CAGR, gap or instrument reading consulted. ADDED BY THE SECOND PASS FOR THIS NATION, 4 cells: bio_cross_sectional_imaging (health and agriculture board), bio_monoclonal_antibody (health and agriculture board), bio_recombinant_pharma (health and agriculture board), core_pcr (health and agriculture board). The refused list above has been reduced by exactly those ids and by nothing else; every other first-pass refusal stands untouched, and each new grant carries its own citation below.

granted.source: Route (b), inherited from comp_microprocessor: World Bank IT.CMP.PCMP.P2 1990 = 15.07 PCs per 100, second-highest in the series after the United States and above every European value.

LIMB A as in the technology note. LIMB B: Advanced Set. CLASS E2: Murray V, 'Improved double-stranded DNA sequencing using the linear polymerase chain reaction', Nucleic Acids Research 1989;17(21):8889 (PMID 2587244), Molecular Sciences Group, Peter MacCallum Cancer Institute, Melbourne, November 1989 - an improvement to a PCR technique, not an adoption of one. Corroborated by 'The application of the polymerase chain reaction to cloning members of the protein tyrosine kinase family', Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Melbourne Tumour Biology Branch, Parkville, Victoria (PMID 2482828), and by PCR haemoglobinopathy diagnostics at the Molecular Biology Laboratory, University of Sydney (PMID 2611144). LIMB C SEARCHED: nothing found.
World Bank IT.CMP.PCMP.P2 1990 = 15.07 PCs per 100, 6.2x the World value and second-highest in the series after the United States.

Oracle established an Australian subsidiary within three years of 1982 (Oracle corporate histories, as above); Australia is also named among the five locations of Oracle's 17 international marketing subsidiaries as at 1986. Australia also holds comp_microprocessor at 15.07 PCs per 100, the second-highest density in the series.

R3: Telecom Australia launched Australia's first cellular network on the AMPS standard in 1987, in Sydney in February and Melbourne in May. World Bank WDI IT.CEL.SETS records 184,943 Australian mobile cellular subscriptions in 1990.

Telecom Australia launched Australia's first cellular network on the AMPS standard in 1987 - Sydney in February, Melbourne in May. World Bank WDI IT.CEL.SETS records 184,943 Australian mobile cellular subscriptions in 1990.

Telecom Australia powered remote microwave repeater stations across the outback from crystalline-silicon arrays from the late 1970s, and Australia had one of the largest remote-area photovoltaic fleets in the world per head by the 1980s - the combination of distance, sunlight and no grid made photovoltaics the cheapest option rather than the green one. FLAGGED: I am confident of the Telecom Australia repeater programme and of Australia's remote-area standing, and less confident of the exact commissioning dates, so this is the third of my three least-certain grants.

LIMB A as in the technology note, and Australia is where limb A is documented by name: the Australian Human Pituitary Hormone Programme, which had treated about 660 Australian children for short stature since 1967, was suspended in 1985 after CJD deaths among hGH recipients (Lazarus L, 'Suspension of the Australian human pituitary hormone programme', Medical Journal of Australia, 1985; Commonwealth inquiry by Associate Professor Margaret Allars). LIMB B: Advanced Set. CLASS E2: Cowell CT, Quigley CA, Moore B, Kirk J et al., 'Growth and growth hormone therapy of children treated for leukaemia', Acta Paediatrica Scandinavica Supplement 1988;343:152-61 (PMID 3195330), Institute of Endocrinology, Children's Hospital, Camperdown, Sydney. THIRTY-SEVEN children 'commenced on SOMATREM' - methionyl recombinant human growth hormone - with mean height velocity reported over the first 6 and 12 months, so administration began in 1986-87 at a named Sydney hospital. LIMB C SEARCHED: nothing found placing Australia outside recombinant-protein prescribing; the pituitary suspension is the reason those children were on a recombinant product at all.
WHO/UNICEF WUENIC DTP3 coverage, Australia, 1990: 95%. Series: WUENIC DTP3 ('Australia,AUS,1990,95').

LIMB A as in the technology note. LIMB B: Advanced Set. CLASS E1 - a published per-country penetration statistic with a date before the board. OTA, 'Health Care Technology and Its Assessment in Eight Countries' (OTA-BP-H-140, February 1995), chapter 2 'Health Care Technology in Australia', reporting the National Health Technology Advisory Panel's synthesis on CT: 'By mid-1987 there were at least 170 CT units in Australia, 118 in the private sector and 52 in the public sector; at that stage, installation of public hospital units had become more widespread. It appeared that on a per capita basis, Australia offered higher levels of CT services (10.8 scanners per million residents) than any European country, but lower than the United States and Japan.' Reimbursement for CT examinations was available through Medicare. MRI in the same chapter: private radiology practices made investment judgments in MRI in the early 1980s, and the government evaluation programme ran at radiology departments in five public hospitals, one study alone reporting 2,810 consecutive examinations at the Royal North Shore Hospital, Sydney, with follow-up on 2,100 cases. LIMB C SEARCHED AND CLEARED: the honest defeater candidate is that Australian MRI density was deliberately held down by the NHTAP assessment and stood at 1.3 units per million, 'a somewhat lower proportion than in several European countries' - but the cell is CT-and-MRI together, MRI was in clinical service at named hospitals, and the CT figure is the highest in the comparison outside the USA and Japan. Grant rests on the MRI-and-conventional-CT half.

NAMED-ARTEFACT BAR, CLASS E2: Kerr PG, Atkins RC, 'The effects of OKT3 therapy on infiltrating lymphocytes in rejecting renal allografts', Transplantation 1989;48(1):33-6 (PMID 2665232), and the same authors' 'The effects of OKT3 anti-rejection therapy on in situ allograft infiltrating lymphocytes', Transplantation Proceedings 1989;21(1 Pt 1):977-8 (PMID 2650302), both Department of Nephrology, Prince Henry's Hospital, Melbourne. These are BIOPSY studies of patients already receiving OKT3 anti-rejection therapy - the therapy is the given, the lymphocytes are the question - which is the clearest possible signature of established clinical use. LIMB C SEARCHED: nothing found.

Australian Customs' EXIT1, enabling exporters to apply for permits electronically, was implemented in 1988 (mandatory from 1991), and the on-line COMPILE customs declaration lodgement system had been in use by customs brokers since the late 1970s. R. Clarke, 'EDI in Australian International Trade and Transport', Bled 1994. DISCLOSED LIMIT: Australia's EDIFACT-based cargo systems all postdate the start date - Tradegate Australia formed 1989, Air Cargo Automation launched 1990 in Sydney, EXIT2 1991, Sea Cargo Automation re-piloted 1993.

Tasmanian Atlantic salmon: Salmon Enterprises of Tasmania (SALTAS) was established in FEBRUARY 1985 as a joint venture between the state government (51%), the Norwegian company Noraqua (19%) and local growers (30%), with a sea farm at Dover in southern Tasmania and a hatchery at Wayatinah; Noraqua harvested the first Tasmanian Atlantic salmon in 1986, and by 1989 Tasmanian salmon was competing with Norwegian suppliers on the Japanese market (University of Tasmania, Companion to Tasmanian History, 'Aquaculture').
